title: Self-Paced Module: Market Analysis and a System Proposal
continues: Week 19 — Advanced Components and User Interaction

lessons.title: Find a Useful Problem and Check the Need

objectives.cognitive: Distinguish a problem, a user need, evidence, an assumption and a proposed feature.
objectives.affective: Respect users and report only what the available evidence supports.
objectives.psychomotor: Write a problem statement, alternatives comparison and evidence record for your own theme.

blocks.markdown: Work in order. Write Activities 1–5 in a notebook or local text file and retain your notes. All work is possible offline using the module, existing programs, observation or labelled scenarios. No survey, paid tool, internet or personal-data collection is required.

**Starting programs and retained files.** Vehicle: run java Main; retain the Week 18 launcher and readiness group, with Week 19’s JComboBox TerminalPanel. School-materials practice: run java RequestDemo; this is the final Preview, Info, Rename and confirmed Clear version. Optional LayoutDemo and ThemeLayoutCheck are earlier demonstrations, not either main program. Retain all model/exception/service/worker files, the five Week 16 helpers and Main_week16.txt, Main_week17.txt and Main_week18.txt. These starting files were recovered by applying Week 19 Steps 1–4 in order. No Java change is assigned this week. The assessment is a proposal for your own existing theme program.

**Course history:** Week 11 classes/objects; 12 four OOP pillars; 13 exceptions; 14 collections; 15 file handling; 16 threads; 17 Swing basics; 18 layout managers/panels; 19 advanced components/user interaction.

A careful look at intended users, their needs and existing alternatives. In this small school project, it helps you judge whether an improvement is useful; it does not require sales forecasts or an invented market size [YD] [IF].
Before adding another counter at a materials desk, find out what learners cannot finish at the current desk. A brighter sign may help more than a new computer.

**Worked classroom scenario, not field research.** Imagine a school-materials desk using loose paper requests. The scenario says some requests omit a subject or collection place. Intended users are learners preparing a request and a desk helper reading it. No interview, survey or count of actual school requests was conducted.

rows: Scenario fact: some paper requests omit a subject.
Given in this exercise; not evidence about our school.
Assumption A1: a complete summary would reduce clarification.
Unverified; compare completion and clarity in a later trial.
Proposed feature R1: show a complete request preview.
A design choice; not proof that users need or prefer it.

blocks.markdown: **User need:** prepare a clear request containing subject, materials and collection place. **Existing alternatives:** keep loose paper; use a labelled paper form; use the existing RequestDemo draft. Paper works without a powered computer. A labelled form may solve missing fields cheaply. RequestDemo can check choices, but does not submit requests, promise stock or save a record.

**Activity 1 | Own-theme need record.** In your notebook, name your existing theme program and one current capability. Write: "[User] needs to [task] because [specific difficulty]." Compare the present/manual process and one other available alternative. Record one item you actually observed, with its context, or label it an assumption and say what would verify it. Do not collect personal details. Finish with one limited improvement and why it may help.

**Check yourself:** "Everyone wants my app" is unsupported. Replace it with a named user group, task and labelled basis. Classmate role-play is classroom feedback, not field research. If evidence is absent, an honest assumption record is acceptable.

**Code verification:** The retained final sources compile with Java 8 compatibility; FareCheck was run. Both launchers return their no-display message when forced headless. A normal launch could not connect to X11; no virtual display is available. Windows, resizing, physical keyboard/clicks and live dialogs were not checked in this preparation.
**Time allocation:** 10 min recall; 20 min explanation; 25 min example comparison; 35 min own-theme record; 20 min review and slip; 10 min revision = 120 min.

2. Yale University [YS]. [Define the Scope](https://usability.yale.edu/ux/plan/define-the-scope). Brief excerpt: “success criteria”. Connect features to needs and keep within resource limits.

3. Iowa State University Extension [IF]. [Feasibility Study Outline](https://www.extension.iastate.edu/Agdm/wholefarm/html/c5-66.html). Brief excerpt: “underlying assumptions”. Compare alternatives and examine assumptions before deciding.

4. Iowa State University Extension [IP]. [Writing a Business Plan](https://www.extension.iastate.edu/agdm/wholefarm/html/c5-68.html). Brief excerpt: “supporting evidence”. Keep the plan honest, consistent and clear.

5. Carnegie Mellon University [CP]. [Proposals](https://www.cmu.edu/student-success/other-resources/handouts/comm-supp-pdfs/proposals.pdf). Brief excerpt: “realistic plan”. Explain the need, scope, resources and completion plan.

**Key validated facts:** Identify a specific user task [YD]; compare alternatives and label assumptions [IF].
After Activity 1, answer the Monday exit slip.

lessons.title: Use SWOT to Make Practical Decisions

objectives.cognitive: Classify specific SWOT entries and explain how the project boundary affects classification.
objectives.affective: Accept a fair challenge to a claim and acknowledge a limitation honestly.
objectives.psychomotor: Complete an own-theme SWOT with a basis and practical action for each entry.

blocks.markdown: A check of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats against one objective. Strengths and weaknesses are internal to the project or team; opportunities and threats come from outside that boundary [CAR].
A materials-desk team can improve its own request form. It cannot guarantee that the school will keep a computer available all afternoon. Name who controls the condition before classifying it.

**Set the boundary first.** For this example, the project is a learner-built, single-computer request-draft tool. The learner controls its code and instructions; school access arrangements and power supply are outside the project. The objective is to prepare a complete draft, not to manage a whole office. The outside conditions below are hypothetical assumptions.

rows: Strength: existing preview checks required choices.
Internal code capability in final RequestDemo; inspect summary().
Reuse the checks instead of redesigning them.
Weakness: drafts disappear when the program closes.
Internal limitation; final RequestDemo has no save/load feature.
Disclose the limit; consider one local save/load improvement.
Opportunity: the school may offer a supervised desk trial.
External possibility, not confirmed permission.
Ask for approval later; use only a classroom simulation now.
Threat: a shared-computer booking may be cancelled.
External access condition, assumed for this scenario.
Keep a labelled paper form as a fallback.

blocks.markdown: **Do more than fill four boxes.** Link a strength to an opportunity: reuse validation during a possible supervised trial. Reduce a weakness against a threat: a save/load option may protect a draft between sessions, but it cannot replace access to a computer. Keep paper available. These decisions depend on a later feasibility check [CAR] [ID].

**Context matters.** "No internet" is a fixed external classroom condition here. It threatens an online-only design, but is not a useful threat entry for a fully offline tool unless you explain its effect. "Our program cannot work offline" is an internal weakness. "Good design" and "many users" are too vague. Replace them with a capability or condition and its basis.

**Activity 2 | Own-theme SWOT.** State your objective and project boundary. Write at least one specific S, W, O and T for your proposed improvement. For each, give evidence or an assumption label, explain its classification and write one action. Add two linked decisions using pairs of entries. Ask a partner to challenge one classification; revise it or explain why it still fits. Record this as classroom feedback.

**Check yourself:** if you write "available laptop", explain whether it is owned/controlled by your team (possible strength) or only a possible school loan (possible opportunity). A classification needs a stated boundary, not just a positive or negative word.
**Plan your own SWOT decisions:** For S, W, O and T, write an entry and basis, why it is internal or external, and a useful action. Finish two linked decisions: use S with O; reduce W against T.
**Time allocation:** 10 min recall; 20 min classification; 25 min worked SWOT; 35 min own-theme SWOT; 20 min partner check and slip; 10 min revision = 120 min.

**Key validated facts:** Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external. Use the entries to choose actions [CAR].
After Activity 2, answer the Tuesday exit slip.

lessons.title: Check Whether the System Is Feasible

objectives.cognitive: Explain technical, operational, economic and schedule feasibility and justify a decision.
objectives.affective: Value realistic commitments, support for users and honest estimates.
objectives.psychomotor: Complete four feasibility checks, calculate costs and make a timed work plan.

blocks.markdown: A reasoned check of whether a proposed solution is practical with available resources. Check all four areas below before recommending proceed, revise or postpone [TO] [IF].
A desk plan needs more than a working form: someone must use it, help when it fails and have time to maintain it.

rows: Technical: can we build and support it?

Existing Java 8 Swing draft and Week 15 file-handling skills support a small local save/load option. JDK and one computer suffice. File validation and safe failure handling still need design and testing.
Operational: could people use and maintain it?
Plan a 30-minute orientation, clear labels and a paper fallback. Learner maintains source; a future desk helper would operate it. Helper availability and permission are assumptions, not commitments.
Economic: are benefits worth resources used?

Compare a labelled paper form with the software improvement. Count supplies, training and maintenance time; existing equipment is not cost-free to operate. Benefit is clearer reusable drafts, not proven money savings.
Schedule: can the work fit available time?

A hypothetical later 8-hour work allowance supports only a small extension. Allocate 1 h design + 3 h save/load + 2 h testing + 0.5 h orientation + 0.5 h notes + 1 h buffer = 8 h. This is not this week's lesson timetable.

blocks.markdown: **Classroom estimates only, not researched prices.** Assume an already available computer and JDK, no new purchase, and shared power covered by the school. That does not prove a real budget. For a one-week trial, assume the following sample supply amounts. Before real use, verify actual prices, equipment access and support.

rows: Orientation card: 2 sheets x P2
P4
P0
Fallback forms: 5 sheets x P2
P0
Added hardware/software purchase: none in scenario
P0
P0
Identified supply subtotal

blocks.markdown: **Recalculate:** first trial week = P4 + P10 = **P14** identified cash outlay. Four trial weeks = P4 + (4 x P10) = **P44**. These are partial supply totals, not total ownership cost. Developer time is included in the 8-hour plan, not priced as a wage. Operator time is estimated separately at 10 minutes per trial day: 5 days x 10 = 50 minutes/week. Power and future repairs are unpriced shared costs, not zero-cost findings.

**Benefit estimate:** assume 10 drafts/week and 1 minute less clarification per draft: 10 x 1 = 10 minutes/week, not observed savings or earnings. This does not by itself justify 50 minutes of operation time. Compare the paper form in a later controlled trial before claiming a net benefit.

**Decision:** revise to a small local draft extension and keep paper fallback; verify access, need and support before a real trial. Proceed only when essential resources and checks are credible. Postpone if a required computer or support is unavailable and no workable smaller scope remains.

**Activity 3 | Own-theme feasibility.** Complete four checks with available/missing resources, evidence or assumptions, a risk and an action. Separate one-time and recurring costs, state a time period, and show arithmetic. If no new cash purchase is needed, explain time and shared resources. Total a realistic work plan with testing and buffer. Choose proceed, revise or postpone and defend it.

**Activity 3 planning record:** For each feasibility area, record available/missing resources, a basis, and a risk/action. Total design, changes, tests, training, notes and buffer within your work allowance. State your decision and reason.
**Time allocation:** 10 min recall; 25 min four checks; 25 min cost/time example; 30 min own-theme feasibility; 20 min review and slip; 10 min revision = 120 min.

objectives.cognitive: Explain how needs, requirements, SWOT, resources and feasibility support one proposal.
objectives.affective: Keep claims modest and protect the time and information of intended users.
objectives.psychomotor: Draft a short proposal for an improvement to your existing own-theme program.

blocks.markdown: A short plan explaining a useful problem, the intended improvement, the supporting basis, resources and a justified next decision. A requirement states what the system must do; scope sets the limits of the work [CP] [YS].
A proposal is the desk team's clear request to try a small change: what it helps, what it needs and what remains uncertain.

**How the pieces fit.** Market analysis identifies the task and alternatives. SWOT exposes useful capabilities and risks. Feasibility checks whether the proposed work is realistic. The proposal combines these findings; a promising idea may still need revision before any implementation [IP].

rows: Clear request draft; scenario missing fields.
R1: retain subject, materials and place validation and Preview.
Missing input is rejected; correction produces a full summary.
Resume a draft; assumption A2, not verified demand.
R2: save/load one local draft using a learner-controlled file; no personal data.
Reload a sample; handle missing/malformed files without losing current valid choices.
Recover safely; existing Week 19 behavior.
R3: retain safe Rename and confirmed Clear; warn before replacing an unsaved draft.
Cancel/No/close preserves current data; replacement requires explicit Yes.

blocks.markdown: **Short proposal example | Hypothetical school-materials draft.** Intended users are a learner preparing a draft and a desk helper reading it. The classroom scenario describes incomplete loose-paper requests; this is not a finding about our school. A labelled paper form is a serious alternative because it needs no powered computer. The existing RequestDemo already previews subject, materials and place. Whether resuming a draft is useful is assumption A2; a later approved trial must check that task.

**Proposed improvement and limits.** Add one local save/load draft option to the existing practice program while keeping R1 and R3. Use invented sample requests and an arbitrary request label, never a classmate's personal data. No online submission, stock promise, database or multiple simultaneous users is included. The current program does not yet save or load files.

**Analysis and resources.** Reusable validation is a strength; no saved draft is a weakness. A possible supervised trial is an external opportunity; cancelled shared-computer access is an external threat. Reuse the controls, limit storage to one file and keep paper fallback. Java/Swing and prior file work make the idea plausible, but safe file handling remains unbuilt. Users would need orientation and a maintainer; neither school adoption nor helper support is confirmed.

**Cost, time and recommendation.** Use Wednesday’s assumptions: P4 one-time supplies, P10/week recurring supplies, P14 first week, plus unpriced shared costs and 50 minutes/week operator time. Plan 8 hours of later development and preparation, including testing and buffer. Benefits remain unverified. **Revise** to this small scope and verify A1/A2, access and support before an approved trial. If safe file handling exceeds the allowance, retain the current draft program and reassess. This example is a proposal, not a completed system.

**Activity 4 | Begin your own proposal.** Use your existing own-theme program, not Vehicle or a renamed copy of RequestDemo. Link three useful requirements to user needs and a later check. Reuse Activities 1–3; resolve contradictions. Use the proposal starter and planning record below. No new Java program is required.
**Check yourself:** a proposed capability must be labelled planned. Compiling an existing program cannot prove demand, adoption, usability or the success of an unbuilt feature.

**Activity 4 continued | Draft review.** Write a short proposal of about 2–3 notebook pages, plus compact tables if needed. Use the same user group, problem and scope in every section. A partner should be able to trace each requirement to a need and see why your decision follows. Record feedback as classroom feedback; revise one weak connection.

blocks.markdown:
**Five-minute presentation**

- 30 s: name your existing theme, user and problem.
- 1 min: compare alternatives; point to evidence or assumptions.
- 1 min: explain a SWOT decision and all four feasibility findings.
- 1 min: show requirements, resource/time plan and recommendation.
- 1 min: answer a question honestly; describe one revision.
- 30 s: state what must be verified before real use.

**Prepare using your own proposal**

- Which claim in your own proposal is least certain?
- Why is the manual alternative insufficient or still useful?
- How does your existing program support one requirement?
- What would you remove if available work time halved?
- What evidence would change your recommendation?

blocks.markdown: For each criterion: full points = complete, specific and justified; about half = partly developed or weakly linked; zero = absent/unrelated. Award intermediate whole points for quality. Give credit for honest assumptions with verification needs. Slip scores are separate.

Start Thursday after the proposal model; complete and present Friday. Write a short proposal of about 2–3 notebook pages plus compact tables if needed. For a large class use circles of at most 12, peer records and teacher rotation. For each rubric criterion: full points = complete, specific and justified; about half = partly developed or weakly linked; zero = absent/unrelated. Award intermediate whole points. Honest assumptions with verification needs earn credit; do not invent evidence. Slip scores are separate.
checklist: Name your existing own-theme program and a current capability.
Define a specific problem, intended users and task.
Compare the manual/current process and another alternative.
Record evidence or labelled assumptions with verification needs.
Give specific S, W, O and T entries, their basis and actions.
Complete technical, operational, economic and schedule checks.
Link three limited requirements to needs and later checks.
Explain resources, costs, time, support and a realistic work plan.
Justify proceed, revise or postpone and state remaining limits.
Present briefly, answer honestly and record one revision.
presentationOutline: 30 s: name your existing theme, user and problem.
1 min: compare alternatives; point to evidence or assumptions.
1 min: explain a SWOT decision and all four feasibility findings.
1 min: show requirements, resource/time plan and recommendation.
1 min: answer a question honestly; describe one revision.
30 s: state what must be verified before real use.
questionsToPrepare: Which claim in your own proposal is least certain?
Why is the manual alternative insufficient or still useful?
How does your existing program support one requirement?
What would you remove if available work time halved?
What evidence would change your recommendation?

rubric.criterion: Problem, users, alternatives and program connection
Four feasibility areas, resources, costs and work plan
Clear presentation, honest answers and revision
